previous_record.title: Black Queen swarms: can less capable individuals make a smarter collective?
previous_record.question: Can selection for cheaper agent policies cause useful individual skills to disappear while collective performance improves through dependence on a few helpers?
previous_record.prediction: When costly outputs are shared, some lineages prune redundant capabilities, improving group performance per budget while losing solo competence; helper removal reveals the new dependence.
previous_record.comparison: Cross inherited capability pruning enabled/disabled with public/private helper outputs. Compare heterogeneous Jev/Haiku/Qwen mixtures, same-model specialists, and a fixed optimizer-designed division of labor. Remove and restore helpers after adaptation.
metrics: Verified task success per total budget
previous_record.falsifier: Drop adaptive-dependence claim if no individual capacity is lost, helper removal has no selective effect, or fixed specialization explains the entire result.
previous_record.confounds: Prune explicit tools, skill files or policy branches, not model weights. Include actual maintenance/context costs and a zero-maintenance control. Selection must not directly reward dependence; retain solo evaluation and matched tool access.
previous_record.delta: Black Queen dependence is established in microbes. Candidate extension is selection-induced loss of agent-side capabilities with a measured group gain and causal public-good dependence across different model interfaces.
previous_record.decision_value: Discover when minimal cheap agents are an efficient ecology and when eliminating one rare helper makes the whole deployment brittle.
previous_record.biophysical_mechanism: Adaptive loss of costly leaky functions; measure cost, inheritance, dependence and frequency change.
previous_record.visualization: Replay a lineage tree whose capability icons disappear, beside a growing dependency graph; mark helper removal and rescue.

previous_record.title: Agent organelles: when does symbiosis become an evolutionary trap?
previous_record.question: Can a Jev decision policy and a generative partner become a jointly inherited unit whose private interface improves familiar performance but prevents adaptation to a new task ecology?
previous_record.prediction: Stable co-inheritance creates partner-specific gains, followed by an adaptation penalty after a task shift; partner exchange or interface normalization may release that constraint.
previous_record.comparison: Cross persistent versus shuffled partners with joint versus separate selection of inherited policies. Add frozen standardized interfaces versus co-adapted interfaces. Test severing, reciprocal partner swaps and a new task distribution without granting extra calls.
metrics: Benefit or damage from interface normalization
previous_record.falsifier: Do not call this an organelle-like transition if dependence is imposed from initialization, any partner works equally well, or the pair adds only the strongest member’s output.
previous_record.confounds: Endosymbiosis and evolutionary lock-in already occur in digital life. External selection copies finite policy/skill bundles, not model weights or autonomous organisms. Paired budgets, interface bandwidth and accumulated history must be matched.
previous_record.delta: Digital organelles are prior art. The narrower gap is whether learned semantic/typed interface compatibility, rather than hard-coded trait matching, causes and releases dependency in heterogeneous inference agents.
previous_record.decision_value: Determine when a tightly paired cheap controller and planner can safely be upgraded independently, and when a successful pairing locks out future capabilities.
previous_record.biophysical_mechanism: Egalitarian transitions, co-inheritance and stabilizing selection from partner compatibility; operational analogy only.
previous_record.visualization: Animate paired lineages, interface compatibility and fitness before and after a task shift; show severing and cross-partner rescue.

previous_record.title: Ecological inheritance: does the habitat decide which agents are intelligent?
previous_record.question: Can agents transform a shared workspace so that it selectively favors their own model family, causing a self-reinforcing change in future population composition?
previous_record.prediction: The same newcomer population performs differently in habitats built by different model mixtures; those effects persist through agent replacement and feed back into which mixture prospers.
previous_record.comparison: Use reciprocal transplants of naive/experienced agents into clean/mature habitats, then cross builder-family A/B with newcomer-family A/B. Equalize underlying information and tool semantics; separately normalize artifact schemas. Compare frozen versus composition-responsive recruitment.
metrics: Verified success at equal context/tool cost
Recruitment feedback and invasion from rarity
previous_record.falsifier: Drop niche-construction claim if gains are generic retrieval for every model, vanish after equivalent information matching, or cannot affect later population composition.
previous_record.confounds: Shared memory, stigmergy and environment inheritance are prior art. Separate easier tasks, extra stored answers, schema familiarity and tool affordances. A dirty workspace is not automatically an ecosystem.
previous_record.delta: Beyond memory reuse or turnover alone: test reciprocal habitat adaptation that changes the relative fitness of model families, and the resulting population feedback.
previous_record.decision_value: Choose portable shared environments versus team-specific infrastructure, and detect path dependence when replacing a model.
previous_record.biophysical_mechanism: Niche construction, ecological inheritance and priority effects, tested by reciprocal transplants.
previous_record.visualization: Replay two landscapes of artifacts and niches; swap entire populations and show which family flourishes in each inherited habitat.
previous_record.literature_overlap: Memory and inheritance strongly covered; model-family habitat feedback remains unconfirmed.

previous_record.title: Cultural speciation: can compatible swarms evolve incompatible ways of thinking?
previous_record.question: Can isolated mixed-model swarms develop co-adapted procedural bundles that work internally but fail when recombined, even after vocabulary and tool schemas are translated?
previous_record.prediction: Low-migration islands develop positive within-lineage procedure interactions and poor cross-lineage hybrids; intermediate migration limits that incompatibility without eliminating useful specialization.
previous_record.comparison: Start islands with identical model mixtures and vary migration. Recombine partners and separately recombine skill modules. Test held-out tasks with an equal-budget dictionary/schema translator, plus randomized unlinked skill bundles and same-model islands.
previous_record.falsifier: Drop speciation analogy if incompatibility is only renamed symbols, unequal model competence, missing documentation, or arbitrary module mismatches equally common in shuffled controls.
previous_record.confounds: Emergent language, strong-to-weak learning and spontaneous social clusters are already demonstrated. Fix model versions and initial mix; no biological reproductive isolation is claimed.
previous_record.delta: Test recombination incompatibility of co-adapted procedures beyond lexical dialects, using translation and linkage-breaking controls.
previous_record.decision_value: Predict when separately successful teams or skill libraries cannot merge, and whether modest exchange prevents fragmentation.
previous_record.biophysical_mechanism: Cultural isolation, migration and epistasis-like interactions among inherited procedures.
previous_record.visualization: Replay diverging islands and skill lineages, then a matrix of successful within-island pairs and failing cross-island hybrids.
previous_record.literature_overlap: Language and clusters established; procedural hybrid breakdown is a candidate distinction.

previous_record.title: Cognitive food webs: can one agent live on another agent’s failed work?
previous_record.question: Can discarded partial work from one model create a resource niche that makes an otherwise dominated cheap model worth keeping?
previous_record.prediction: A cheap consumer that cannot compete from scratch contributes verified solutions by transforming failed-but-partially-valid donor artifacts; removing that byproduct stream eliminates its advantage.
previous_record.comparison: Give consumers budget-matched failed fragments, shuffled fragments, successful trajectories, or no donor artifacts. Remove and restore byproducts, compare copying versus transformation, and test whether the consumer can invade from a low resource share.
metrics: Marginal verified solutions from failed artifacts
previous_record.falsifier: Drop food-web claim if benefits are ordinary retrieval of completed answers, extra sampling budget, or a niche assigned by the harness rather than earned through marginal contribution.
previous_record.confounds: Trajectory markets and bacterial cross-feeding are prior art. A failed whole solution can contain useful local information; independently verify fragments and account for the cost of producing waste.
previous_record.delta: Causal dependence on transformed failed work sustaining a useful cheap-model niche; reuse alone is insufficient.
previous_record.decision_value: Find cheap agents that earn their place by recovering value from expensive failures, and distinguish them from redundant extra attempts.
previous_record.biophysical_mechanism: Byproduct cross-feeding and resource-mediated coexistence; information is reusable, unlike consumed nutrients, so depletion must not be presumed.
previous_record.visualization: Animate provenance flows from failed donor artifacts through transformations into verified outputs, alongside niche shares.
previous_record.literature_overlap: Strong reuse overlap; transformation and sustained resource dependence are the proposed distinction.
